utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. May it please the Court, two small issues. First, there are some preliminary matters, I think that they were alluded to a week ago, that need to be addressed. And we would greatly appreciate it if the Court could keep in mind that we would prefer to have these issues addressed sooner rather than later; for example the dead, unwilling and unavailable witnesses. We think that those issues serve no one's interest by being left hanging, and we would appreciate it if the Court would carve aside, perhaps, an hour to discuss these and some other issues that we would like to bring up at some convenient point. Secondly, the next witness is Major Mark William Bower. We have just received a copy of the offer of proof, which is 24 pages in length. From looking at the proposed testimony of this witness, we would like to make some applications before the Court. First, the testimony of this witness seems to be almost completely duplicative of the testimony of Lee Whitworth, who was also a liaison officer with the first battalion of the Prince of Wales Own Regiment, just as is Major Bower. Their time on the territory pretty much overlapped and it appears to me, from a brief scrutiny of the document that we've just been given, that the testimony is almost completely duplicative of that offered by former Captain Whitworth. Therefore, in terms of considerations of time and so forth, we would object to his testifying at all. But if he's permitted to testify, there are three or four areas where I think that the Court has already heard substantial evidence on matters that are nowhere charged in the amended indictment. Let me be specific. First, there is the issue relating to the Convoy of Joy on June the 10th and 11th, 1993. This matter was already addressed at length by Mr. Whitworth and by other witnesses. I don't think that it needs to be addressed any further. Especially when it's completely outside the specific events charged in the amended indictment. Second, there are some statements made from -- made by an interpreter about whom the Court has already heard evidence, Dobrila Kolaba, who is obviously not available to be cross-examined and those statements need to be assessed for reliability in due course. Obviously, provided the appropriate foundation can be laid, then perhaps the evidence may be admitted. But we just want the Court to be aware that there are double hearsay concerns connected with some of those statements. Third, there are two incidents which -- about which the Court has already heard extensive evidence. The actual killing of Ms. Kolaba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Sayers. Excuse me, Mr. Sayers. Could you tell us each time the number which is involved in respect of the questions that you are speaking about, so that we can follow it on the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll do my best. I apologise for flipping through this, but I've just been give the document and I haven't had a chance to scrutinise it carefully. With respect to Ms. Kolaba, I believe that's page 20, paragraph 135, 136, 137, and 138. Another issue about which the Trial Chamber has already heard extensive evidence is the HVO assault on the Grbavica feature on September the 8th, and that's addressed at paragraphs 140 to 150. Once again we would point out to the Trial Chamber that that incident is nowhere specifically alluded to in the amended indictment and since it's of peripheral relevance anyway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it in dispute, that there was such an assault?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, which is one additional reason, Your Honour, why we object to any further cumulative unnecessary testimony on this. And there is also, and I don't have it readily to hand. Perhaps the Prosecution can help me. There is further testimony about the shooting incident involving the UNHCR driver identified by the name of Boris and some conclusions that emerge from that. I think Mr. Whitworth has already gone into that. It's not disputed that the gentleman was shot. It's not charged anywhere in the amended indictment and I simply do not think and we would submit to the Court that it is not necessary to hear any more evidence on that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll get Mr. Scott to deal with details of Mr. Bower's evidence, because he's been dealing with him. I thought you would like to know what the position about witnesses is generally for this week, although I think there's been a letter setting our position out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We had very, very considerable difficulties because two substantial witnesses pulled out at the last minute for reasons that were good for them and probably are good, given that they have competing international responsibilities, I think. In any event, they pulled out. There are four witnesses available for this week. This is the first. There's objection taken to one of them by the defence, Schipper, because he -- although listed, wasn't identified until the last minute or relatively last minute last week as somebody we intended to call this week. We've made arrangements to have him here. We hope the defence can cooperate. Because without that witness, there was every probability that time would otherwise not be used. We simply couldn't find anybody else to fill the gaps that were being left by these two witnesses who let us down. We've managed to make available another witness, who was seen last week in Bosnia, and I don't believe there is any objection to his being called. So there are four witnesses for this week of five sessions. And I'll get Mr. Scott to deal specifically with the objections taken now by Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be sensible to try and deal with the matters of law this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I can deal with that position -- it would be sensible, but I'm not sure that it's possible. As the Court will remember from what I explained earlier, we have to have our final position witness by witness on unwillingness. Now, this week I've been actively involved in dealing with one or two particular unwilling witnesses and in pursuing the alternative remedies that there may be available to us. And, of course, we take -- we move step by step before we are ultimately in the position of saying this witness is unwilling. We don't want to say this witness is unwilling, we want to compel the witness or persuade the witness to come by every means at our disposal, including, where appropriate, the issue of subpoena. We have to decide whether to attempt to compel appearance by subpoena or to decide that it's not an appropriate case, and if it's not an appropriate case, to take the next steps, witness by witness. And I don't think I'm going to be in the position with any particular witness to say that we've come to the end of that road. That's the only reason that we are not in a position to go ahead with the unwilling witnesses. Ideally, I should like never to have to present the argument, because I'd like to be able to have every witness here or, alternatively, to have them available to give evidence by one of the alternative methods available. So I regret I'm not sure that it is possible to deal with that argument at this stage, much though it would be otherwise desirable to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it be possible to deal with the argument in relation to dead witnesses? No question that we can deal with that. So it would be sensible to leave aside an hour or so and get through that during the week. I suppose as far as the unwilling witnesses are concerned, it's not really a matter for the -- not a matter for the defence, it's not really a matter for the Court. It's your application.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's our application, if and when we feel we have to make it. But we are progressing everything logically and with an eye to getting witnesses here, wherever possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, when you come to the end of the road, I would certainly advise you to make the application as early as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We certainly will. I'll let Mr. Scott then deal with this witness. The only other alternative matter is the question of a Court view of the area, but that can no doubt be fitted in at some convenient time and probably better in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Again, we'll try and deal with it this week. Mr. Scott, speaking for myself, if you had in mind at this point about repetitive evidence and would avoid it, unless you consider it essential. It's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. We have considered it. It's somewhat of a challenge to take a -- witness bits and pieces of a witness on part of a story with no context.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. We are sensitive to that, Your Honour, and we will try to eliminate as much as we can -- I apologise for not being on the microphone. It is difficult, simply, to jump from one assertion to another without a certain amount of contextual reference as to where this witness was, how this witness was involved in a particular event. The Convoy of Joy, Your Honour, let me just indicate, is no more than three paragraphs of this outline. There is a video that this witness is familiar with, which has not been shown before. It is new evidence, by any definition. In terms of the interpreter statements, Your Honour, we think they are the type of statements which this Court has received before. We are talking about statements directly within the scope of the interpreter, if I can put it this way, the interpreter/interpretee relationship, her part of her professional duties to work with Major Bower and to keep him so informed. In terms of her unfortunate murder, Your Honour, there are certain aspects to some of these events. It's not just simply that the event itself is undisputed. It's one thing to say, yes, we agree this woman was killed, but there are aspects in which it happened which we believe are significant as to broader issues. It's our contention, Your Honour, that there was, at this time in Central Bosnia and many locations, a concerted coordinated sniper campaign. Not the actions of any individual soldiers. It's highly unlikely that someone as insensitive as U.N. personnel would have been targeted by an individual soldier without some authorisation or clearance at a higher level. And that this interpreter was standing beneath -- literally standing beneath an U.N. flag in the BritBat house, officer's house, when she was shot and killed. We believe there are aspects other than the mere event of her death which is significant evidence. In reference to Mr. Sayers' point about the killing of a Muslim civilian immediately following the attack on Grbavica, which I can cite for the record is the same as the village of Divjak, it's one of these locations, Your Honour, which there is more than one reference. Some people call it Divjak, some people call it Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I was looking for it on the map. We have not been able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's exactly the reason, Your Honour. It's unfortunate now in retrospect and, frankly, I have to give Ms. Verhaag the credit for reminding me this morning, it's unfortunate that the outline speaks in terms of Grbavica. I guess I did that because that's the term the witness uses. But it is Divjak which, by the way Your Honour, is in fact in the four corners of the indictment. This one situation where this one person was killed, again, Your Honour, it's one paragraph. It is apparently not disputed. So I don't think we need to worry about taking a great deal of time. So I think we can move through it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may just have one word. I will not repeat anything which was said. I'm just a little bit afraid that we might have a problem with discovery material related to the witness. It is obvious, at least I suspect, that in an earlier statement given to the investigators the witness is obviously following his notes. We have not been given any kind of notes, diaries, whatever it was. And I would like to have a clear statement from the Prosecutor whether they have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The answer is no, Your Honour, we do not. We've never had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Major Bowers, is it correct your full name for the record is Mark William Bower?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it's correct, sir, that you are a career officer of the British army; you joined the army in approximately 1983; you've now served something like 16 years. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your current rank is Major and you are presently assigned as a staff officer at the headquarters of the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Germany; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your military experience, sir, you have served in Northern Ireland, Kuwait, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Canada, Kenya, France, and the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reference to some of those countries which we can probably identify by name, you were involved in combat duty during the Gulf War; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with your time in service in Bosnia, Major, is it correct that you were awarded The Queen's Gallantry Medal?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that in fact you've just returned from a second tour of duty, if you will, into the former Yugoslavia, having spent approximately six months with British peace-keeping forces in Kosovo, from approximately the 27th of March this year to 5 October 1999?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Major, is it correct that in connection with your former tour in Yugoslavia, you first arrived there as a member of the BritBat forces in Split, Croatia, on the 24th of April 1993 as a member of the Prince of Wale's Own Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I arrived at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please pause between question and answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll remind both of us, Major, and it's probably I'm the biggest offender, that because we both speak the same language, we both probably need to pause and slow down for the interpretation into the other languages. The Prince of Wales Regiment, is it correct, was the BritBat unit, if you will, that followed the Cheshire Regiment which had been commanded by Colonel Bob Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It did follow it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, at that particular time, sir, is it correct you were a captain in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were assigned to the BritBat camp near Vitez and took over there as the G-5 liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In this position, you were responsible for humanitarian matters in BritBat's area of responsibility, you were the liaison officer involved with and assisting, essentially, the humanitarian organisations working in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And some of the organisations, just to give the Court some greater feel for that, you would work with such organisations as the Red Cross, UNHCR, and such organisations or units as that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Major Bower, your tour there lasted until the 7th of November, 1993, and during most of this time you worked in the areas of Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As part of the -- well, were you, in fact, given some briefing and training or orientation, if you will, on your arrival or even prior to your arrival in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, we received training.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have an understanding that the commander of the HVO, Central Bosnia Operational Zone, was a man named Colonel Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, we were briefed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know then and come to have personal experience that confirmed that Colonel Blaskic had his headquarters in the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, during the tour I became aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear on this point, Major, is it correct that you personally did not have any dealings with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be a fair comment, in general, as relating to your testimony this morning, that the way the contacts or liaison frequently occurred or regularly occurred was that there was some contact at a corresponding level, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, for instance, your commanding officer was General Duncan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, he was our commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it would be more likely, for instance, and do you know in your experience, in fact, that Officer Duncan, Mr. Duncan, had, in fact, contact with not only Mr. Blaskic or Colonel Blaskic, to your knowledge, but also with one of the defendants, Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In the evening briefs, the evening updates that we had, the commanding officer would always brief us on what he had done that day, give us his thoughts. And in those briefs, he would mention the people that he had met, and the names of Blaskic and Kordic arose during those briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, what did you know, in a similar fashion as I've just asked you about Colonel Blaskic, what did you know about Dario Kordic and who he was and where he fit into the picture?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was briefed to us in the military information summaries and the evening updates that Dario Kordic was on the political side of the HVO part of the conflict at that time. He was much more of a political figure than a military figure, on the same level as General Blaskic. And therefore it was generally the commanding officer who would meet with him, and so I did not meet with Mr. Kordic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that a term that you used, in describing what you just now told me, was that Dario Kordic was the political face of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's an accurate reflection of the briefings which we were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court -- or let me ask you -- is it correct that in your experience, events in the Lasva Valley were controlled at the very highest levels at a military, political, strategic level?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was certainly the impression which I gained over the six months that control was at the highest level. There appeared to be little flexibility for military initiative at the extreme lowest level, which is generally where I was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, in your experience and based on your observations, that very few decisions were made at a lower level, even tactically, by local commanders?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's right. It was certainly apparent that if a decision was required, it would have to be referred up the HVO military chain to get the decision overturned if, for instance, it was to get through an HVO blockade where they had been told not to allow UNPROFOR to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct to say, Major Bower, that it was your assessment or that it appeared to you that this was some sort of a characterisation or carry-over, if you will, from the Communist system where command and control was centrally located in the hands of a few people?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly, it was my impression that it was a carry-over, that control was held centrally within a small number of people rather than allowed to be disseminated and personal initiative to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was it true, in your experience and the assessment of the British Battalion and the British forces in Bosnia, that among those people, if you will, in whose hands power resided included Dario Kordic and Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to that question, to the extent that it calls for the rendition of a conclusion and an opinion. Major Bower has already testified, Your Honour, that he never met either now General then Colonel Blaskic or Dario Kordic, and so I don't think any rendition of any opinion along these lines would be particularly helpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Except for this, that the witness may have experience from which he can speak of these matters. It may be that it was gained at secondhand, but nonetheless if he's got some experience, he can tell us about it. Mr. Scott, if you would like to establish a foundation for any opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Major, you've already indicated and is it correct that there were essentially nightly briefing sessions among the various liaison officers and your Commanding Officer Duncan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Every night for the complete tour, we were there at 18.00 hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would you consider these briefings to be rather thorough?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: They were in-depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, was it essential to your day-to-day tasks to be fully briefed on day-to-day events?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: To allow the liaison officers to make correct judgements or judgements at the time which would not impede or hinder any of the other liaison officers, it was felt that we should know exactly what was happening on a day-to-day basis, not only on the military level but also on the local political level, so that anything which we did with relation to humanitarian aid agencies or any of our liaison duties would not come into conflict with any policy which at the time was being used higher up the chain of command within UNPROFOR or the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that in these nightly briefings, Mr. Kordic's name was mentioned frequently?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kordic's name was mentioned frequently. Whenever he had been met by any member of the battalion, then always it was reported back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, with that additional foundation, is it correct, sir, that among these people who were in the command and control position in the Lasva Valley, again based on your observations and experience in Bosnia, did those people include both Colonel Blaskic and Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, I must object to that question because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can give -- it's a matter of weight. It's a matter of weight. The witness is going to tell us, no doubt, the impression that he gained from the briefings which he attended.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. It was certainly my impression, from the briefings and also from my time on the ground on a daily basis, that the high levels were involved in decision making.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's move forward and let's just clarify the situation for the record as to the person who is the other defendant in this proceeding, Mario Cerkez. You knew who Mr. Cerkez was, in terms of someone who was also active in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. Again from the nightly briefings and the training before we deployed, I was aware of who the local brigade commanders were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It would be fair to say, in summary, -- on this point I think it's fair, Your Honour, to say -- that while you knew and may perhaps have had some contacts with Mr. Cerkez, you might say, on an incidental basis, he was not someone who you had any particular dealings with, any significant dealings with, during your tour in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. If I met Mr. Cerkez, it was purely by accident. It was by no means anything that was designed. It was normally because I would be wanting to meet with another liaison officer who may have been in the vicinity. I had no direct dealings with Mr. Cerkez at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving on, is it correct that about the end of April 1993, perhaps the 26th or 27th, you accompanied the Cheshire Regiment, which was still in Bosnia at that time perhaps during a transition time, to assist in the recovery of some of the bodies there?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you find that although the massacre at Ahmici had been, by that date, committed some days earlier, the clean-up operation was taking some time?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The delay in the clear-up was for fear of unexploded munitions that were in the area which were hindering the collection of the last few bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct that from what you saw at the end of April, that the attack on Ahmici appeared to have been a concentrated military effort that had been quite brutal in its execution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think again we've heard evidence on this topic from the people who were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Let me skip several paragraphs, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you see or did you hear that of the remaining or untouched houses in Ahmici, that these were the houses where the Bosnian Croats, as opposed to the Muslims, lived or had lived?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As you toured Ahmici at that time at the end of April, is it fair to say that you did not see any evidence of military fortifications in or around the village in terms of trench works, weapons pits, or that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's move on to a particular group in the HVO. Did you come to know an organisation or group of people called HOS or H-O-S?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of their presence from the nightly briefings and came into contact with them through my duties as a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in your experience and based on what you heard in the briefings, these HOS soldiers typically wore black or perhaps very dark blue uniforms, they seemed to be always clean and in good order, seemed not to be hungry in the sense of having been perhaps under more destitute or hardship conditions, they wore HVO insignias on their uniforms, some wore white belts with a white cross-belt over the chest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in your experience, these HOS soldiers tended to drive Western European cars such as, in particular, Volkswagen Golfs?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why is it that was, if it was, particularly noticeable or remarkable to you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It stood out just because it was different. The appearance, the bearing of the individuals, were different from the normal conscript HVO soldiers which I came into contact with, the fact that any car that was driving around would be of interest, that more so if it was a Western European car, because petrol, diesel, was a fairly sought-after commodity at that particular time. Whoever had access to that sort of petroleum or diesel would normally be of importance and therefore of interest to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your experience and BritBat's assessment that the people who tended to have fuel for their vehicles tended to be, as you say, the more important people such as the politicians, the military commanders, and some of the more favoured units?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that was generally the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that during your tour, you saw HOS soldiers or elements throughout the Lasva Valley frequently between the T-junction at Novi Travnik and the T-junction in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that was the majority of the times when I would see them, either statically at checkpoints or driving around in their cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that you, on occasion, saw HOS soldiers at Colonel Blaskic's headquarters at the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think you just mentioned -- in terms of their driving around in cars, would they do something -- did you observe them or come to know that they would do something called a "snap checkpoint"? Maybe that's not the exact correct term, but something like that?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The terminology "a snap checkpoint" or a control point, "snap" basically for us would mean that it was mobile. It would normally be put on the main routes and transiting through to check who was moving around on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct in your observation, Major, that the so-called HOS groups or soldiers and the HVO regular soldiers were seen together and HOS soldiers moved freely among the other HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly, there appeared to be no restrictions on their movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you at any time see any sort of hostility between the two groups as if the two groups were somehow distinct or opposed to one another?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that they were opposed to each other. They moved freely. They were, certainly as far as we were aware, on the same side, and any hostility between the two groups I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You considered them to be part of the one in the same side?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I am going to skip paragraph 28, Your Honour. Going back to your reference to Colonel Blaskic and the HVO headquarters. Is it fair to say, sir, that you were in the HVO headquarters, that is the Central Bosnia operative zone headquarters, at the Hotel Vitez something like 40 or 50 times during your tour?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. Those figures are approximately correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that you found in your experience the headquarters and its operations to be professional, efficient, and that it was a working military headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The impression which I gained from my experience was that is a correct summary of how the headquarters appeared to function to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, again based on your experience, which we'll get to in the course of this morning dealing with various humanitarian issues, dealing with obtaining passage, dealing with checkpoint issues, was it clear to you that there was in fact a working HVO chain of command and an effective network of HVO communications and coordination?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Most definitely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I think I'll save some particular instances of that as we get further into your testimony. Now, did you come to know that there was -- the HVO had something called, in military terms I suppose, a HIP-style helicopter that made frequent flights into the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. We could view it from our base in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it fair that that was the only aircraft, or at least one of only very, very few aircrafts, that you saw and that BritBat saw in the Lasva Valley during your tour?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give the Court, perhaps not a precise number, but did you see this and know of this helicopter being in the area, we are talking once or twice in a six-month period, or approximately how often?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: During the summer, I would say approximately no more than a dozen times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is a HIP-style helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It is a Russian make of troop carrying helicopter. It is not normally used in the ground attack role. It is merely for ferrying troops. It may be able to carry as many as 18 people, depending on the load.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the end of May or May 1993 to a particular incident. Did there come a situation around that time that you, your driver, interpreter, and in fact a second vehicle were driving on a dirt road in the mountains west of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The incident was -- it was a fact finding mission. We had not been in theatre for very long. The UNHCR had requested information on what was around west of Busovaca and, therefore, my call signs were driving -- we just followed our noses. There was no particular specific place to go. We were just heading west up the mountain track when we came to a tree across the road which had been cut down. As we stopped, I got out of the vehicle. I noticed on my right-hand side there was a chalet, hunting lodge type building set in the trees some distance from the track. A dozen or so well-armed and competent soldiers, who later became identified as HVO soldiers, took up firing positions around us and came to identify who we were. Although they wouldn't engage directly in conversation with us, they talked amongst themselves, and in a professional, competent manner, checked us out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me for going back. Before we move entirely forward, I am reminded to ask you -- it may not have been clear on the transcript. The helicopter that you observed some dozen times or so, this was a helicopter associated with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What caused you to associate the helicopter with the HVO, as opposed to, say, the BiH?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The proximity of where it landed and also Darko Gelic referred to it on one particular time saying that it had brought in some particular equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we've jumped a bit ahead in our outline in terms of Mr. Gelic. You better identify him to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: He was the liaison officer from Hotel Vitez headquarters to the BritBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Liaison officer for Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And he had identified this helicopter as in fact being a HVO supply helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: He mentioned that it had brought in some equipment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, in returning to your story, let me again momentarily stop you again just primarily for the education of all of us in the courtroom and in case this term comes out in other evidence or documents. When someone refers to a soft-skinned vehicle, is that a reference that it is essentially like a private vehicle, it is not armoured?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct. It has no armour protection whatsoever. For all intents and purposes, it is an open-topped four wheel drive vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, go ahead. I'm sorry, go ahead if you would and continue with the testimony concerning this group that came out and stopped you.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The group would not engage directly in conversation with me through my interpreter. They attempted to look in the back of both vehicles, which was a policy we tended not to allow. At no point did the whole group surround us, only six or so, and they were always moving in pairs. They left six or so soldiers some distance, 20, 30 metres away, who had taken up firing positions. They didn't move from that. It was quite clear to me that it was an aggressive stance. After some time of going around the vehicle, talking to themselves, my interpreter told me that we should leave and we should leave now. It was quite clear that she was agitated, and I had not seen her like that before. So I bowed to her experience and we extracted from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you a few additional details about this group. You've indicated they were well armed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. They did not all carry the standard Soviet AK-47 assault rifle. There was some German made Hekler and Koch rifles. There was some pistols in holsters, and of the soldiers that came close to me, the vast majority had large hunting knives, which was something that you didn't normally see on the conscript HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that their uniforms were typically well maintained; they had boots; they had something called elastics in the ankles of their trousers; they came across as a very well equipped and trained outfit?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. If I say they looked the part, they had an air of competence and also of aggression, and part of that was borne by the way they carried themselves and also the equipment and the clothing which they had. It set them apart from the normal conscript HVO which I dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that some of the soldiers in this group had black headbands with skull and cross bone insignia on them, while others had similar insignia on the uniforms themselves?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. A small number had the headbands, some had sort of patches on their jackets, and some had patches on their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did some of these patches also indicate HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. There were one or two of the red and white chequered patches on shoulders and also on the jerkins they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've already taken us a certain distance forward. When you were able to extract yourselves, did any of these HVO soldiers say anything to you through your interpreter, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: When we had extracted from the area and gone back down to the outskirts of Busovaca, I stopped the vehicles and wanted to speak to my interpreter to find out why she expressly said that we should leave. She explained that she had heard a discussion between two of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, on the grounds of hearsay and conclusions. There is no contemporaneous translation of comments that were made or of a -- conversations that they heard in the presence of Major Bower, but simply a conclusory [sic] Recitation of opinions that the witness derived from other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As I understand it, the witness is going to relay what the interpreter said to him. So that, of course, is hearsay, but we on the whole allow hearsay. We shall let it in.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I asked her why we should leave, and she said that she had heard a discussion between two of the soldiers saying, "Should we kill them or let them go?" She also stated to me that she believed the soldiers to be from the Jokeri or the Jokers, and she said that did I know who they were. Obviously, from the nightly briefings which we had after the Ahmici incident, I was aware that there was a band of soldiers known as the Jokeri or the Jokers who had been used or did use fairly extreme methods of violence in their attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, as you approached the point where these soldiers came out from the chalet and talked to you, were you proceeding -- if you recall these details, were you proceeding in an easterly direction, that is toward Busovaca, or were you proceeding west from Busovaca from the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I was heading in a generally northwesterly direction from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask the usher now to provide the witness, and I would direct the Court to Exhibit 2624, which is a map, Your Honour, that Major Bower will use at various points in his testimony to orient this to various locations. And it should be in the bundle, I hope, of the documents that's been given to the Judges. First of all, just to orient us on the map. Can you just point out on the ELMO, if you will, where the city of Vitez is located on this particular map?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It's in this area here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For some reason, Your Honour, we are not getting the monitor feed or our machines. In any event, I'll proceed. The area that you encountered these soldiers, have you marked that as approximately the area number 1 on Exhibit 2624?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it fair to say, sir, that that's generally an approximation on a relatively large scale map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. After some years, it's the general area that I seem to remember that we were in at the particular time. I was more concerned with what was happening around me than actually seeing where I was on a map on a track.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is not a scale on this particular excerpt, unfortunately, or legend. Based on your experience in the area, can you, looking at again Vitez and approximately the town of Busovaca, perhaps, and again by way of orientation you can point out on the map where Busovaca is located. What is the approximate distance between Vitez and Busovaca, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: In kilometres along the road, maybe 10, 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What would be the approximate distance? And I know for these current purposes we'll just have to do a rough line of flight, if you will, you might say as the bird flies, but what's the approximate distance from where you saw these Jokers to the town of Busovaca, as indicated on 2624?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I would approximate maybe four or five kilometres. The way the roads were and how we travel, we travelled relatively slowly over ground, which wasn't hard, hard road, for fear of mines. And so time and distance was sometimes difficult to judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, sir, that again based on these briefings, your discussions with Duncan, et cetera, that you knew or came to know that Dario Kordic had a headquarters near Busovaca that some people called the Eagle's Nest?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I was aware of the Eagle's Nest as it was referred to by Colonel Duncan, but its exact location I was just aware that it was in the Busovaca area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back to your interchange -- exchange with your interpreter. She identified these soldiers as being Jokers, and did she tell you that in fact that she had overheard them talking among themselves while they were surrounding your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's how she informed me afterwards, that they had been discussing, should they kill us or let us go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, during your tour did you become familiar with another location associated with the group called the Jokers at something called another lodge or chalet?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. On the main road between Vitez and Busovaca and the Zenica on the left-hand side of the road. If we were travelling in an easterly direction, there was a chalet which, for a period of time, was used as -- or was used by the Jokeri. Whether it was their headquarters, I don't know, but it was used by the Jokers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that the location marked as approximately item 2 on Exhibit 2624?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Approximately here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, some small number of kilometres from Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly travel time, it wouldn't take very long to get from there to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, Major, that based on this particular experience and the briefings and your other observations, that you knew that, in fact, the Jokers then were -- operated actively in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: At this particular moment in time of the tour then, yes, it was certainly the Busovaca area, although we were briefed that they had been seen around the Lasva Valley, but generally were located around Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The assessments that you've made or the descriptions you've given the Court in the last few minutes about these being a particularly professional appearing, motivated group, was this just your assessment or was that again the BritBat military assessment of this group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was the opinion of the majority of the liaison officers and the military information officers who had either come into contact with them or the reports that they had received from various sources about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be a fair description of your knowledge of this group that the Jokers were often used in a vanguard or lead element role in various actions by HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. That's the information which we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that again, based on your information, that the Jokers and in fact there was another -- did you know that there was another type of special unit, if you will, somebody called or some group called the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I was aware of a second group called Vitezovi, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was it your assessment and the British Battalion's assessment that the Jokers and the Vitezovi typically worked jointly with other HVO units and, in fact, that they were observed or encountered as part of joint operations in areas such as Novi Travnik, Grbavica, and Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Major, I want to turn to your role more as the humanitarian liaison officer, which will take us most of the balance of your testimony. In starting that, would it be fair to say to the Court that you found that in your experience that often the HVO side or the Bosniak Croat side was less helpful to you, less -- did less to facilitate your work than, say, the ABiH did?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I would say that in the intense periods of the fighting, June, July, August, I was hindered by the HVO in trying to conduct my main role, which was assisting the humanitarian effort of the aid agencies within that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, part of your role and responsibilities in particular that you spent a great deal of time on was to provide assistance to Muslims who had been cut off in the area or part of Vitez known as Stari Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. That particular enclave occupied a great deal of my time during the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at that particular time did -- was that enclave entirely surrounded by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the HVO controlled, in fact, all access into and out of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. There was only one road to take a vehicle into Stari Vitez and it was controlled and at times the road was closed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, is it fair, sir, that prior to the outbreak of conflict at least by the spring of 1993, while there had been two roads or ways into Stari Vitez, but one of these had been blocked more or less permanently sometime earlier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I don't know the exact date when it was blocked, but the western edge of Stari Vitez was blocked on the road by some earthworks piled up on the road. There was the trailer of a lorry dragged across the road and what looked like artillery shells, explosives linked by detonation cord on the road. It was a pointless task trying to get round it or go through it and, therefore, we always used the access to Stari Vitez or Vitez via what was known as the Vitez T-junction, which was to the eastern edge of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am going to show you a map in a moment, or an aerial photograph. Is it correct, sir, that the Hotel Vitez, which was Colonel Blaskic's headquarters, that was located only some 500 or 600 metres from the front line, if you will, of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. It was very close to the front line or no man's land of Vitez, Stari Vitez between HVO and ABiH forces. Travel time in a Land Rover, the vehicle I was in, 30 seconds, one minute to get from Hotel Vitez into Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher's assistance in distributing a large aerial photograph. Try putting it on the easel, Your Honour. I don't know that we can really work with it by way of the ELMO, because it's too large, but we can try with the easel and perhaps we can also give out copies. It's a bit large, Your Honour, and somewhat unwieldy, but I think it's the best illustration of the items that Major Bower is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for it being somewhat oversized, but again it was the best tool that we could find for these particular purposes. There is a legend on the map. With the Court's permission, Major, you might stand and approach or you could point and be seated, whatever you're most comfortable with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you show us on the map, first of all, if you'll look in the lower left-hand corner just to orient, because the map is -- sometimes we tend to think of things up and down as being north and south, but if you look at the lower left-hand corner of the map, could you show us the orientation north?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: [Witness complies].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, the appearance of the map is somewhat counter-intuitive to the extent that we assume that up is north, but in fact the upper side of this aerial photograph is south; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Or somewhat south. Again, it's at an angle. All right. Could you show on this map where Hotel Vitez was located?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Just here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you point out the area of Stari Vitez? What we're looking at overall is a large part of the town of Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. This is showing Stari Vitez [indicates], which is in this area here you can see the fortifications which would be part of the front line, and this area here [indicates] into Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where was the point of access, if you will, the HVO roadblock or point of access actually into the enclave of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: There was never any manned checkpoint between the hotel and access -- this access road [indicates] into Stari Vitez. What would generally happen, mines would be placed across this road, which would obviously mean we couldn't take any vehicles through there, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask the question perhaps a little differently. Where, on that road, did you consider that you had crossed over, if you will, from the HVO side to the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: There was a small sort of area here [indicates] which there had been quite a large bomb had gone off, the houses were derelict, and that to us denoted the front line crossing from one military-controlled area into the other. I would say approximately in this area here [indicates]. It's difficult to tell now after some time and looking at it above rather than from side to side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Again, to give us all some sense of scale, when you testified a few minutes ago that Hotel Vitez --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You testified a few minutes ago, Major, that Hotel Vitez was approximately 500 or 600 metres from Stari Vitez, and is that -- in discussing that distance, are you talking about the difference between Point A on the photograph and again this approximate confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly until I had left the car park here in Hotel Vitez at Point A, 30 seconds to a minute, 500 metres, before I was within the ABiH-controlled area of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just a few other things about this particular map. Item B is the Cinema Vitez. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not asking the witness, Your Honour, but I think it's fair to comment at this point in the record that the Court will note that that was Mr. Cerkez's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you point out to the Court on this map the approximate site of what came to be known as the truck bomb? There had been a truck bomb incident in Stari Vitez. At that Point I?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. This was the point I referred to earlier where the houses surrounding it were derelict and tended to denote where we would cross from one military-controlled area into another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think we can move on from that particular aerial for now. It may come up later. Let me direct your attention next to an excerpt of this, which is considerably handier, 2174. Now, there is a bold yellow highlight marker on this Exhibit 2174, and can you tell the Court, does that represent your path, if you will, your path of transit from the Hotel Vitez to what was called the hospital in Stari Vitez where you were actively involved in evacuating casualties?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I would enter through what became known as the main street past the site of the lorry bomb until we got into virtually the centre of Stari Vitez, where I would then go off to the north, where there would then be the hospital. It was just off the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, what was called the hospital being just barely -- just on the bottom of the photograph, is that correct, "bottom" in the sense if we're looking at the letters A, B, et cetera, oriented appropriately for reading?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This was called a hospital. Was it, in fact, or had it, in fact, before this been a hospital?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It wasn't a hospital by the definition of what you would expect. It was a house or a store which had been converted into a makeshift medical centre where casualties could be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward with your testimony outline, is it correct, Major, that you tried a number of times to evacuate wounded Muslims out of Stari Vitez, but the HVO checkpoints were ordered by their chain of command to stop and search your vehicle, for instance, to be sure that you were not transporting people out of the town?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. We were prevented on a number of occasions from entering Stari Vitez to evacuate casualties. The reasons given generally were either, "We want to search your vehicle and to make sure you're not taking casualties out," or they would just deny us access completely and not allow us in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, during this particular time, and I realise it may have changed from time to time, but were there times in the summer of 1993 that the humanitarian organisations such as the Red Cross, such as the UNHCR, would not go into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. When the -- the fighting was unpredictable, and their safety, as they travelled in again soft-skinned, non-armoured civilian vehicles, could not be guaranteed. The UNHCR and ICRC would actually just refuse to go into Stari Vitez to collect the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that those duties, even though they were of a humanitarian nature, fell primarily to the British Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: There was nobody else that was going into or would attempt to get into Stari Vitez, so inevitably it fell to either myself or another liaison officer to attempt to evacuate the wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you encounter, during your tour of duty specifically in connection with Stari Vitez, a denial of access to Stari Vitez and other similar villages for the purpose of providing humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't just the evacuation of wounded people. It was delivery of the whole strata of humanitarian aid, whether it be food or medical supplies. There were times when UNHCR, ICRC, would not be allowed in. My vehicles did not have the capacity and neither did UNPROFOR feel it right that we should be doing the UNHCR's job of delivering the quantity -- the tons of aid required. It was something of a precedent we didn't want to get involved in. We were trying to get the aid agencies to actively participate, but it was a very difficult time in some of the areas. Understandably, their position against the threat assessment. So it was basically left to negotiations from UNPROFOR, the British Battalion, the aid agencies, with various military sides to effect humanitarian assistance. And it was not always successful, and I would say it was through no part of ours. We were attempting it, but the conditions were just not right, they weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The resistance that you encountered in terms of providing access, evacuating casualties, did you find that in your experience to be something on a random or sporadic basis or was it your assessment that this was part of a policy or strategy?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The denial of access into Stari Vitez tended to be linked to whatever could be happening militarily on the ground within the Lasva Valley. It was sometimes linked to fighting elsewhere in the Lasva Valley and sometimes it was denied due to fighting physically between the two sides in Vitez. Sometimes it was linked to the evacuation of Croat civilian casualties from the hospital in Nova Bila, which I was also involved in. So it fluctuated, but it seemed to be controlled at a high level because it was always where we had to go, the higher level, to get the issues resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your particular experience, when you say where you had to go, where was it you had to go to get authorisations or access into Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Ultimately, we had to go to the Hotel Vitez to get the decisions or to get the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it correct, sir, that despite these very difficult conditions, that you were, during your tour, able to evacuate approximately 50 to 60 critically-ill or injured Muslims from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, approximately I would say it was, over the six months, that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that most of these were women and children and that most of them would likely have died if they had not been evacuated?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly, the criteria which I tried to put on the evacuation, if the ICRC or UNHCR would not accompany me, would be that they could not receive the medical attention that they required if they were to stay in Stari Vitez. Therefore, I would attempt to move them. A lot of it was based on my personal decision at the time, depending on the situation between the Stari Vitez hospital and travelling by road ultimately to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you find that the types of injuries or casualties that you encountered in Stari Vitez were largely of two sorts, one being gunshot wounds and the other being blast wounds or, if you will, shrapnel from explosions?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, the vast majority of injuries which I saw, the casualties which I evacuated, were what I would term battle trauma, either gunshot wounds, blast injuries. There were a minority of what I would say were day-to-day medical conditions, broken limbs, inoculations which were required, those sort of evacuations, but they were the minority. The vast majority were battle trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that it was the assessment of the British Battalion that the HVO, in connection with Stari Vitez, was conducting a coordinated sniper campaign against the Muslims in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. It was our opinion that there was a policy, a deliberate policy, of sniping at the population within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A sniper can be, in your terms, Major, anyone who waits for a target of opportunity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. A sniper does not necessarily have to be somebody with a custom-built sniper rifle who is well concealed. It is anybody who takes a target of opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. As you've just indicated, while perhaps not what we think of in our minds, especially of the civilians, as a sniper weapon, can an AK-47 serve as a sniper weapon?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Any weapon can be used. The term "sniper" is something which I would not necessarily use in this context. Any weapon can be used to intimidate or attempt to shoot targets of opportunity in an area, if you're prepared to wait long enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Using the AK-47 in a sniping role, perhaps we can put it that way, is the accuracy of such a weapon that it would be, again other than area fire, if I can use that terminology, but to be used to target very specific targets, is the effective range something like 150 to 200 metres?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The rifle does not come with an optical sight, and therefore its effective range individually is approximately 150 metres; a good shot, possibly 200 metres. But at that distance, you should be able to see what it is you're shooting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For instance, sir, and based on your military training, at 150 metres you should be able to see if you're shooting at a Bosniak soldier or if you're shooting at a woman or child; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly, I feel that the distinction between a grown adult and a child would be visible at that distance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Covering some particular incidents, on the 23rd of June, 1993, is it correct that you went to the Stari Vitez hospital, you saw a middle-aged Bosnian Muslim woman brought in who had been shot by a sniper, she was already dead, and when you spoke to the doctor, the doctor told you that this was the second civilian sniper on that particular day, sniper victim, and the doctor told you that she was not able to travel -- that is, the doctor was not able to travel outside of Stari Vitez because of the threat posed by the Bosnian Croat snipers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that on one afternoon in May, an 11-year-old Muslim girl was shot through the head by sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know whether she survived?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, she did. We evacuated her to Zenica hospital, and some six weeks later we tracked her parents down and reunited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did there come a time when a UNHCR representative was shot and killed in Stari Vitez while sitting in a marked UNHCR vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that incident happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the type of weapon that was used to kill this driver?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was a high-calibre, high-powered rifle which was a 12,7 or 50-calibre sniper rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court whether that is -- was that a weapon issued to a common soldier?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: From our experience, it was a weapon of prestige. There were not many known to be in the Lasva Valley, and therefore its use was singularly important because it was a weapon that was not generally available to HVO conscript soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just by point of reference, sir, can you tell us the status of that weapon, or weapon like that, in terms of it being issued and used in the British army?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: If it was the equivalent in the British army, as a company commander of 100 men, I would have four snipers in my company, and they worked direct to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your experience, a sniper with this type of weapon would be closely controlled by a commanding officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct the usher or ask the usher, please, to show you what has been entered as Exhibit 2773 which was admitted by a prior witness, 2773. Mr. President, Mr. Nice has just reminded me again just to make clear that we have unfortunately no access to the monitor, so we'll continue, but if there's anything that could be done about that, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The photograph that is marked as Exhibit 2773, do you see a 50-calibre sniper rifle in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see the -- I think you've been handed the wrong photograph. It should look like this [indicates]. Perhaps it's our numbering mistake. 2773.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 2773.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We'll mark this one. Mr. Usher, if you could, please, hand the witness this, we'll mark it. Your Honour, we'll find the appropriate number and reassign it and make it part of the record. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Major, do you see a 50-calibre sniper rifle in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's the one which is being held vertically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were you present when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how was it that you were able to get this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: As you can see, the soldier holding it is actually looking through a British army rifle here, and most soldiers the world round are always interested in seeing other weapons they are not familiar with, and that was a way of getting to look at the rifle. It's a common practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, in other words, is it fair, Major, that you or one of the people with you had handed this HVO soldier a British rifle essentially for the purpose of taking his attention while you photographed the sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. There was some individuals who were wary of having photographs taken, which is understandable, but this was a way of also getting a balance of scale between two weapons, as best we could, in the same photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, when you come to a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you, but we've certainly seen this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can no doubt, during the adjournment, track it down as to what the number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. A couple more questions, and then we can close and, before moving on, take our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This soldier that's holding the rifle, was he identified to you or to your group as, in fact, a HVO sniper?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: He was identified to us by the sheer fact that the badge which he has on his tunic and the fact that he was looking after that weapon, to us signified that he was a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately where this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I can't remember now, I'm afraid, where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. We can stop there, Your Honour, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now until half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with our thanks to the Registry, we are able to confirm that the photograph of the sniper rifle is indeed Z2773.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before moving on, Major, the vehicle that the UNHCR driver was in when he was shot and killed, was it marked as an UNHCR vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Large letters along the side of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that the effect of this one single shot was to stop all humanitarian relief convoys into Stari Vitez for at least the following two weeks?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The UNHCR were affected quite badly by this incident. And it pretty much stopped all UNHCR activity within the Lasva Valley for approximately one to two weeks. It was not something which they had expected and it took some considerable reassurance by UNPROFOR to get them to continue with their activities. But from then on the UNHCR were very wary about going into any area which was not quite as stable as they would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did they insist on BritBat escorts?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly into Stari Vitez and to anywhere near a front line they requested direct UNPROFOR escorts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that to the extent this reflected additional duties on the part of the British Battalion's part, that this, given scarce resources, kept them from doing something else?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The British Battalion had been trying to encourage the aid agencies to work independently on their own rather than rely on direct escorts, because that was very intensive for our vehicles and our manpower. We tried to create the conditions where they could go about their business without direct escorts and therefore we could cover a larger area of ground with the same number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct sir, that a sniping campaign is psychologically damaging and in fact has a very demoralising effect?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes.
