The whole purpose of attrition by a small number of individuals can have a deep, psychological impact on soldiers as well as civilians, and certainly in the case of Stari Vitez the systematic attempts to prevent the civilian population from going about their day-to-day business of trying to maintain their crops and their own independent food supplies by the use of snipers meant they had to conduct a lot of their outside activities at night. So this again has a psychological impact on the individuals concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your assessment, Major, that many of the attacks on the population in Stari Vitez were either deliberately targeted at civilians or the result of indiscriminate fire?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly from the indirect weapons, mortars, whatever, then it was an indiscriminate targeting or policy, but certainly the use of a direct weapon like a rifle, to me indicates a fairly direct policy of attrition, of psychologically trying to intimidate a civil population. By the sheer fact that the majority of the casualties which I was involved in were definitely non-combatants and by being women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving, in fact, to the issue of indirect fire. Is it correct that another major cause of the injuries or deaths to Muslim civilians in Stari Vitez was from blast or shrapnel injuries?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The majority of the collateral damage and some of the civilian casualties were created by blast injuries created by explosives of indirect weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your experience, did the indirect weapons consist of both mortar fire, in the sense of traditional or actual military weapon, call it a mortar, and also something that became known as fire extinguisher bombs?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The use of professionally manufactured military mortars of varying calibres were employed, but also the homemade, what we would term homemade or locally produced mortars, utilising fire extinguisher canisters which we referred to as fire extinguisher mortars or fire extinguisher bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your experience, would these canisters typically filled with either gasoline or petrol, to make an incendiary bomb or an explosion, create blast injuries?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The two types encountered, which we were informed about, were the blast or explosive filled or the incendiary device with whatever ignition substance was used to create the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the approximate range of these fire extinguisher bombs was something like 100 to 200 metres?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, they were a very short range weapon, although we had no or I had no direct involvement of where the baseplate or the firing point was, but I certainly saw the results of the receiving end of such devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court how these fire extinguisher bombs were actually fired?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The process to launch these locally produced mortars would be to have a tube slightly larger than a fire extinguisher to ignite a substance to ballistically launch or throw the projectile the desired distance of 150 to 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I am going to direct your attention, please, to Exhibit Z2039, which should be distributed, I think. It's on the ELMO, or I hope the Court will also have copies. What is depicted there in Exhibit Z2039?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That looks like the casing, the fire extinguisher, which would be the actual projectile which would be thrown or ballistically launched from the baseplate to the receiving point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the accuracy of these weapons, Major?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: They were not particularly accurate in the terms of how I would describe military produced weapons. There were no guiding things, it's homemade, and therefore it all depends on the way the system is used, how hurriedly it is produced, how the baseplate, the launching point, is dug in. Not a particularly accurate weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were they fairly slow in flight, and obviously this would vary from particular targeting, but generally speaking slow in flight from the time of being fired until the time of impact?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. Any mortar is traditionally a slow weapon. It's trajectory, obviously, is deemed by the range which is required. But it is not a swift weapon of one or two seconds. It would take some time from launch to detonation at the contact point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What is the effect or consequence of that, in terms of the weapon in fact hitting what it was you originally were shooting at?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I would say that from my experience these types of weapons are -- they are not accurate. You cannot guarantee that it will hit what you intend it to hit. It is an area weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Given the situation in Stari Vitez, which we might not be able to fully appreciate just looking at the aerial photograph, which is still on the easel, but in your experience, was it often the case that these fire extinguisher bombs and mortars, for that matter, were being fired over buildings, that is buildings that intervene between the firing point and the impact point?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly line of sight from the firing point to the contact point would not necessarily be available. So you were firing it over obstacles, over buildings or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So there again you could not be at all assured whether you were firing at civilians or whether you were firing at a military target?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Having said that, was it in your experience the case that the impacts of these fire extinguisher bombs was frequently some distance away from what you knew were in fact the combat lines?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The few times I was in Stari Vitez when this system was employed, I was unaware of where the military actually were, but certainly on a number of occasions they certainly landed in the habitation area or where the civil population or the population lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's correct, sir, that on the 17th of July 1993 you evacuated three Bosnian Muslim civilians, a man, woman, and child from Stari Vitez who were all wounded by shrapnel from mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the man died?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you touched on this earlier. When you wanted access to Stari Vitez, you went to the Hotel Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: If the entry point or the checkpoints into Vitez or Stari Vitez didn't allow us access, then, yes, I would have to go to Hotel Vitez to negotiate entry into Stari Vitez. If there was no hindrance, then I would just drive straight in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the person who you typically came to deal with at HVO headquarters was Darko Gelic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You described him earlier as a liaison officer for Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember which month, but it was after we had constantly been going into Hotel Vitez, I think it was decided to make a single point of contact in Hotel Vitez where the UNPROFOR could always go to build up almost a personal relationship, so then it would speed things along and make things more reliable because we started to get to know how people worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your experience that Mr. Gelic himself could give you approval or authorisation right away?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: No. It was certainly the case that we would go and make a request and it would be discussed with Darko Gelic, and then he would invariably leave and discuss elsewhere and come back and give us a decision. He was sort of the first point of contact for us in Hotel Vitez, but very rarely did he actually say immediately "Yes" or "No" to our requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing you to the 1st of June, 1993, is it correct, sir, that you were contacted by the Merhamet aid representative in Stari Vitez, who said that she was very concerned because the HVO had deliberately stopped all aid going into Stari Vitez and that her main concern was the small hospital there which badly needed medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever I went into Stari Vitez, I would always go to the hospital but also to the Merhamet representative within Stari Vitez just to see how things were, because again they were a focal point who could give me the general situation as to humanitarian supplies within Stari Vitez, because if anybody delivered aid, it would always be within their presence. So they could give me indications as to how the population were doing, and generally they were realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to try to pick up the pace a bit, Major. Is it correct that on the 19th of July, 1993, after some substantial difficulty, you and Captain Whitworth were, in fact, able to evacuate some seven wounded Bosnian Muslim civilians from Stari Vitez to the hospital in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Around the 26th of July of 1993, did you learn that there had been some direction from the HVO in Mostar to the effect that the HVO would prevent any further Red Cross convoys from moving unless the HVO in Novi Travnik was allowed to receive aid?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that was made known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You learned that through the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. Every morning, I would go to the ICRC headquarters in Zenica, and they made it known to me at one of their briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in your assessment, the HVO practices, in connection with Stari Vitez we've discussed so far this morning, could, in the obstruction of humanitarian aid, use a sniper campaign, the use of indiscriminate mortar fire and the fire extinguisher bombs, cause the result of either serious injury or death of many Muslim civilians in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it did cause the deaths of people in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you gain an appreciation that the people in Stari Vitez were in any sense being used as a leverage or a bargaining point?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly, it was implied that they were there for leverage against the ABiH who were outside the Vitez pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether it was common knowledge that the HVO chain of command had ordered that Bosnian Muslims not be allowed to leave Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, and it was made known to me at the checkpoints when I tried to enter Stari Vitez on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there any particular incident or conversation which supported -- further supported the notion that essentially the Muslim civilian population in Stari Vitez was being held hostage?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The threats were implied that should anything -- should any concerted effort by ABiH forces be made against Vitez, then Stari Vitez would suffer, and that was alluded to a number of times throughout the summer of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on the 18th of July, 1993, did you have one such conversation with Mr. Gelic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly it was Mr. Gelic that implied that Stari Vitez, I think he said, would suffer should further ABiH attacks be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Gelic saying something to the effect that essentially the HVO would end the fighting in Stari Vitez when they were ready to end the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly, the -- it was implied that they were -- sorry, the HVO were in control and could end whatever or could do whatever they wanted to whenever they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your military assessment, did the HVO have sufficient military resources in the area of Stari Vitez to defeat whatever ABiH forces might have been there?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I think the resources could have been made available to precipitate and take any aggressive action to a conclusion for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking back at Exhibit -- we'll use the smaller version because it's so much easier for everyone -- at Exhibit 2174, sir, given the proximity of both the HVO headquarters for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone at Point A and the headquarters for the Vitez Brigade at Point B, can you tell the Court your assessment of whether it would have been possible to be or work at either of those locations day after day throughout 1993 and not be aware of what was happening in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I would find it very difficult to believe that individuals in those locations would not be aware or even be interested in what was happening some five or six hundred metres away from them. Any expenditure of ammunition generally makes someone interested to know in which direction it's travelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in particular by about mid-1993, the provision of humanitarian aid and evacuation of casualties in Central Bosnia, surely, and perhaps even more widely than that, had become a high-profile and international issue?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. Organised evacuation casualties or evacuation of casualties had become relatively high profile. As it was always to get something like a large evacuation going or organised, it invariably met at the highest levels of the command to get authority to do so, because invariably it would cross a number of front lines and involve a number of various organisations, and media were involved, and therefore it was immediately catapulted into a fairly high-profile event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your experience, did these issues -- were these issues driven and did they require resolution at the very top levels of the various sides?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: In my experiences of the larger evacuations within the Lasva Valley, certainly it was never resolved at the lower levels of command, it was always resolved at the highest levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you relate to the Court your assessment, and any particular examples if they come to mind, in which you saw the Bosnian Croat side specifically linked to the provision of humanitarian aid and evacuation of casualties on the one hand and a military or political programme on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The evacuation of casualties from a hospital in Nova Bila was linked to delivery of humanitarian aid, but it was also linked to, more importantly, military operations in trying to negotiate a ceasefire to cross various front lines to evacuate 50 or 60 civilians to Kiseljak, and it was made quite clear on one particular occasion that the ceasefire would not be forthcoming because the HVO were in the opinion where I believe that the term used was, "We're winning, and therefore you'll get a ceasefire when we're ready."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, please, to Exhibit 1213. First of all, could you first tell the Court what Exhibit 1213 is?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It's a daily milinfo -- military information summary which was produced by the military information cell within the British Battalion. The designation "1 PWO" is the title of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were these reports essentially prepared and distributed on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The reports were produced at the end of every day by the military information officer and were distributed throughout the UNPROFOR chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to about the middle of that -- perhaps a little above the middle of the page. Did it come to your attention that on about the 25th of September, 1993, a U.N. civilian -- excuse me, civil affairs officer had met with Dario Kordic to discuss access to Stari Vitez, which by that time again was still being obstructed by the HVO by means of mines across the road, and it was reported to you or to the British Battalion that Dario Kordic had said access will be denied until the ABiH cease their attacks in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to that question, Your Honour, on the ground that it lacks foundation. I don't think that the Prosecution has actually laid a foundation either that the Major spoke to Mr. Kordic or that the Major spoke to the gentleman that reported this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is clear from the document. In fact, what's happening is that the document is being produced and it speaks for itself. What weight we give it, of course, will be a matter for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just one point of information, sir. Do you know the identity of this U.N. civil affairs officer who met with Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And he lived in the camp with us and he shared an office with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That was an American citizen, Mr. Randy Rhodes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And these reports, these milinfosums, were again the type of reports and documents that were routinely used by the British Battalion and, for that matter, UNPROFOR forces generally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just so the record is clear, did you at any time attempt to smuggle or supply weapons or ammunitions into the Bosnian Muslim enclave of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at any time, to your knowledge, did any humanitarian aid organisation transport munitions into Stari Vitez during your tour?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on the Bosnian Croat side, if you will, did you become involved in efforts to evacuate wounded and injured from the Nova Bila hospital involving Bosnian Croat victims?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during those efforts is it correct, sir, that the hospital administrator there wanted you to take other people besides the seriously ill and wounded, take other people out from that area as part of your convoy, if you will?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: On one particular occasion, yes, it was suggested that I should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know who these people were that the administrator wanted you to take out?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I got the impression that they were relatives of some of the people that were going to be evacuated, but also people who had no connection at all with the wounded that we were trying to evacuate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you exercising or following strict guidelines yourself in terms of only evacuating the seriously wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I tried to apply the same rules the International Red Cross applied, but also the allowance for doing these evacuations was quite involved, as 3rd Corps, BiH headquarters in Zenica also had to give their approval. So there was certain guidelines, procedures, which had to be strictly adhered to, with the production of lists of names agreed by both sides, and impartial observers to identify that the people on the list were the people that were being loaded onto the vehicles. So it was quite a lengthy and protracted process.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that when you refused the administrator's request that he threatened you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. It was made very clear that I personally would physically suffer if I didn't do what was asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it was in connection with this particular incident that you were awarded The Queen's Gallantry Medal?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. Fortunately, the conversation was cut short because the hospital was mortared at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you proceeded nonetheless to take Bosnian Croat wounded out of the area?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Turning to another area called Kruscica. Did you become involved with this village in a similar fashion to, in some ways, your involvement at Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. In the early part of the tour, to assist the ICRC and UNHCR in delivery of humanitarian aid, I was involved in attempting to get through certain roadblocks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And directing your attention to Exhibit 2624, which is the small map, not the photograph, but the map. Is the area marked 4 on Exhibit 2624 roughly south, southeast of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Or, excuse me. West, south, southwest. Is it correct, sir -- Your Honour, in an attempt to move us along, I am going to lead through here until Defence counsel objects. Is it correct, sir, that the HVO troops who usually manned a checkpoint in connection with access to Kruscica, there was a checkpoint there, but it appeared to you that they were orchestrating women and children in the area to obstruct access to Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that one of the HVO soldiers on the side of the road was someone that you came to know as Captain Nikola -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That was the name that he gave me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it clear to you that this Nikola and the HVO soldiers were in fact directing what the women and children were doing?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how do you draw that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: During the protracted negotiations of some three to four hours to try and gain entry into Kruscica, the local or the ring leaders of the blockade, the women, would invariably leave the group, go and speak to Captain Nikola, and then come back and then continue the negotiation in a different way. To me it appeared that they kept going to either confirm or to report back as to what was being negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this did not appear to you, in fact, to be a spontaneous uprising of civilian women and children?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After some negotiations you were allowed through, correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. To start with, the negotiations would last two or three hours, but after that they tended to get longer and longer, and the agreements to get through would get more and more protracted, but invariably we would get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 17th of May, sir, you again attempted to reach Kruscica to provide medical aid to two badly injured Bosnian Muslim civilians from the village who had been hit by sniper fire. You again ran into a roadblock of the Bosnian Croat women and children, after some hours you were able to gain access to Kruscica, but by that time two of the victims had died. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The following day, on the 18th of May, you tried to reach Kruscica again, you again ran into the roadblock of women and children. This time the roadblock had been reinforced, if you will, by the presence of mines on the road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On a particular occasion did you attempt to walk through, if you will, the women and children by standing in front of your Land Rover and essentially walking slowly through the crowd with the attempt to have the Land Rover then follow you through at a slow speed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I did attempt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The soldiers either side of us opened fire over our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 20th of May is it correct that you accompanied the Red Cross, a convoy trying to reach again the Muslim civilians of Kruscica. At the HVO checkpoint, the convoy was stopped, the HVO Commander, again this Nikola, refused to allow the convoy to pass, despite the fact that there had been some 25 tonnes of aid delivered in fact to the HVO side in Vitez around that time?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was, on a previous attempt to get through, one of the complaints was that aid had not been delivered to the Caritas warehouse in Vitez. So, therefore, to try and allay that and put that one aside, I arranged that aid would be delivered and some 25 tonnes were delivered, but again allowance to transit through the checkpoint, a different reason was given, so we couldn't go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that not only that you presumably were expressing some concern over being continually obstructed and delayed, but, to your knowledge, was the British Battalion chain of command passing complaints or protest to the HVO chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Very much so. After one or two attempts of not being able to get through, I personally briefed my commanding officer, General Duncan, who I believe took this issue up with his -- or with Hotel Vitez, whoever he spoke to there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Typically, again at this idea of commensurate levels, was it General Duncan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your observation and experience that General Duncan would then typically deal directly at his level with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. There were definite levels of who would deal with who. And it was generally General Duncan who would deal with Colonel Blaskic at his level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 24th of May 1993, you were again prevented from crossing into Kruscica by a HVO commander who said he would not allow any aid to pass unless the HVO also received aid?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 27th of May you met with the mayor of Vitez, Ivica Santic, to discuss the problems that had occurred during this previous week, the ones that we have been talking about in the last few minutes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During that conversation, did Mr. Santic keep making references to an alleged videotape possessed by the HVO that "proved" that the UNHCR was supplying weapons and ammunition to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. During this time, reference was continually made to a video which proved, apparently, that UNPROFOR or aid agencies were delivering weapons, arms, to the BiH forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you understand that this video was supposedly taken at a HVO checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, apparently it had been taken at a checkpoint, but I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you specifically ask Captain Nikola to show you this video so that you could actually see this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. On a number of occasions I requested to have access to this video, so that I could see what was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At any time was the video produced to you?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: No. The video was never produced. And, again, in my -- my interpreter informed me that the video, in discussions that she had heard, that the video was propaganda. It didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, just to clarify that. When you would be in these various conversations or stopped at a checkpoint, your interpreter would actually be able to hear other conversations taking place among various HVO soldiers perhaps standing around your vehicle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. When you are negotiating over three, four hours, you tend to take breaks, and at that point my interpreter would obviously listen to what was being discussed around her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, it was based on that that she related to you that the conversations among the HVO people themselves were that there was in fact no such video?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to eliminate any evidence, but in the interests of time I will skip past 123 and 124. I would like to direct your attention, Major, to the Convoy of Joy. In your responsibilities as the humanitarian liaison officer for the British Battalion, did you become involved in various efforts to assist or work with the Convoy of Joy?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. Once the Convoy of Joy had been engaged with firing stopped, it was then over to me to try and assist in evacuation of some of the wounded that had been received in that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the Court has heard, and I don't want to repeat it. This was a very large convoy that had been organised starting in Split, Croatia, ultimately intended for Tuzla; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that specific regard did you become involved in transporting four of the wounded Muslim civilian drivers who had been driving some of the aid trucks in the Convoy of Joy?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. I evacuated a number of casualties. I think it was three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you understand who had imposed or caused these casualties?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The local HVO forces in the Lasva Valley had caused the casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in fact the rules of engagement that was imposed on the British Battalion at this time and all UNPROFOR forces made it very difficult to defend the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Not only our rules of engagement, but also our mandate at that time did not allow us to assist in such a direct role with the Convoy of Joy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Nonetheless, sir, is it fair to say, just as a point of historical note, that in this particular instance British Battalion forces were fired on, and in the process of returning fire some HVO soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was this one of the first times in which, in terms of direct combat, if you will, UNPROFOR forces had inflicted casualties on any of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. It was pretty much a turning point for us as a British Battalion on U.N. duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this point I would like the booth to assist us by showing a video which has been marked as Exhibit 2173. There is a transcript that should have been distributed that goes along with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is no sound at this point, Your Honour. There is some footage at the end, which will stop momentarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Major, approximately one third of the way through the video, there was one spot of a British soldier pointing his rifle down the road and then lowering his weapon. Was that one of your men?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that was Corporal Nigel Bulmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you find yourself frustrated because of your inability to prevent this situation?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. It was the first time, really, that our mandate and rules of engagement were exposed to be not quite as effective as we had hoped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on, in the summer of 1993, is it correct, sir, that you saw, in the hills around Novi Travnik, that HVO soldiers were forcing Bosnian Muslim civilians to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand that you were driving by in the course of other duties and came across a group of approximately 15 Bosnian Muslim men who were digging a large trench system while they were being guarded by armed HVO soldiers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On Exhibit 2624, is that the area that's been marked as "5"?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that during your tour, you saw on several occasions that the HVO often used their military police to guard ABiH prisoners, the prisoners -- excuse me -- the guards dressed in military uniforms, the civilians that you observed being in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did the HVO military police, at least on some occasions, wear white waist belts and white cross-belts, such as over a shoulder or chest, that was distinctive?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you attempt to slow your vehicle down on this particular occasion and get a better idea of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened when you did that?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was made clear to me that we shouldn't stop and we should continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I move to this very quickly. On the 5th of July, 1993, at about 8.30 p.m., was there an unfortunate situation where your interpreter, in fact the woman who had been with you at many of the events that we've talked about up until now, that she was shot and killed by an HVO sniper?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you there when she was killed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where was she when she was shot?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: She was -- stood outside the captain's accommodation, the house by the entrance to the British Battalion. It was in the evening, and a group of us were discussing what had happened that day outside of the house, when some shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This was essentially BritBat property or UNPROFOR property, where she was located? I don't mean that in the sense of ownership but in the sense of use and control.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of houses that were used to accommodate the officers and the military doctors from the British Battalion. It was adjacent to the British camp, and the owners of those houses lived there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it common knowledge that this was a location being used by the British Battalion for housing?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was made very clear. We had a very large U.N. flag hanging from an upstairs window. That flag was directly above where we were sitting at the time when the interpreter was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And she was killed, sir, by a single shot to the head from a 7,62-millimetre round from an HVO position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it determined that this HVO firing point was about 150 metres from the house?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, approximately that sort of distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your assessment, sir, the U.N. flag that was flying over your interpreter's head at the time she was killed, could that plainly be viewed from the location from which the fire was directed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: If the group of us and the interpreter could be seen, there is no way that the flag couldn't be seen. But it was also common knowledge by this time of our tour that that was a U.N. house. We had had trouble with snipers before using areas around us, and it had been made clear by Colonel Duncan, the commanding officer, that there was a 400-metre exclusion zone around the camp and they should not be actively engaged in firing anywhere near us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your interpreter was a local woman of mixed Muslim/Serb ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Her parents at the time lived in Novi Travnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I believe you've indicated before that one of them was a Muslim and one of them was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based on your experience over the previous months, had you come to know whether your interpreter was particularly liked or disliked by the HVO in the area?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I got the impression that there were times when her presence was less than favourable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you were sitting out on the -- again in the area right about the time the shot was fired, those of you among BritBat were wearing your BritBat uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It was general practice that we did not put on civilian clothes while we were on duty or deployed in Bosnia, but the interpreter and the majority of the civilian interpreters liked to put civilian clothing back on in the evenings when they were off duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But the group of you as a whole, in addition to being under a U.N. flag, she was surrounded by people in British uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the British Battalion commanding officer make a formal complaint at Colonel Blaskic's headquarters about this interpreter being killed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware of any conclusion or outcome of such an investigation, if any?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: No, I'm unaware of any conclusion that was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you aware of any HVO soldier or person who was punished or disciplined for having killed the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I'm unaware of any action having taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct you back now and tie two events together. When the UNHCR worker was killed at Kruscica or, excuse me, in Stari Vitez, sitting inside the vehicle, and when your interpreter was killed, given the circumstances in Bosnia at the time, would not that have been something of some sensitivity, to specifically target essentially, broadly speaking, U.N. personnel?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Most definitely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at least one of these soldiers was armed with a very special weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, in the case of the UNHCR worker in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based on your military experience, would a decision have been made to kill those kind of individuals by an individual soldier or would that have been the result of command action?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: I would have thought it would be command action rather than a decision at the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the 7th and 9th of September, 1993, the HVO attacked the village immediately adjacent, essentially, to the BritBat camp called Grbavica, which is also, I think, sometimes known as Divjak; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, you and I certainly refer to it as Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This was a town or village which had, up to this time, been somewhat ethnically mixed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And directing your attention back to Exhibit 2624, this is the area marked on the map as Area or Item 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There were a number of houses in the village, including many that were immediately around the British Battalion camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did the Muslim civilian population and perhaps Croat population live in these houses?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At least for the first part of the attack, sir, and then in the aftermath of the attack, did you see various parts of the assault on the Bosnian Croat houses just outside of the British Battalion camp?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were you able to see, in contrast, the Bosnian Croat houses were untouched?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Certainly after the fighting had finished, it was clear to see which houses had been engaged and which ones hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it the after-action assessment, if you will, of the British Battalion that the houses that were left standing were houses in which resided Bosnian Croat families?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After the attack, did you notice that these houses, many of them, were looted and burned after having been cleansed of the Muslim occupants?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The houses which were still standing were certainly looted to the point where someone actually tried to come and loot the house which we were living in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: HVO soldiers actually entered your house to loot it, to attempt to loot it?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I take it they were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: We were still in residence at the time, and they were asked to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it your assessment of this attack on Grbavica that it was a well organised and professional attack?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: It certainly gave the impression of being well coordinated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall some of your colleagues, in fact, commenting, on watching the attack, that it was like watching a training video?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that comment was made. It was a very competent military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the evening of 8th September 1993, sir, did British Battalion forces transport a group of Bosnian Muslim civilians near the village to Travnik to prevent them from being killed, even after the battle, by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. A group of local Muslims were moved to a reception centre in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And here again, sir, in the course of that event or again after the initial attack, there was an incident where one Muslim civilian man who had survived the attack was conversing with two British Battalion officers, and as he was standing talking to the officers in British uniforms, he was shot and killed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that incident did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to conclude on that, after the attack, the HVO military forces essentially moved away and the houses themselves became occupied by Bosnian Croats within 24 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like you to look very briefly at Exhibits 1782 and 1782,1, which are colour photographs or copies of the same. Are both those photographs, sir, pictures taken of the village of -- at least parts of the village of Grbavica after the HVO attack?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, toward the end of your tour, sir, on the 26th of October, 1993, were you advised by British Battalion headquarters that you might have to travel to another Bosnian Muslim village called Stupni Do in a few hours because of a reported HVO massacre there a few days earlier?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on, in fact, the 27th of October, the next day, did you set off in a Land Rover, with other British Battalion components, to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were approximately two hours behind A Company which had departed earlier under the command of Major Roy Hunter?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that on your way into Stupni Do, the Land Rovers were stopped at a well-manned HVO checkpoint outside of Vares, near Stupni Do, and the HVO soldiers there were wearing regular HVO uniforms and were heavily equipped?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You and the others were originally prevented from passing the checkpoint into Stupni Do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, we were prevented to start with, but after a period of negotiation, we were allowed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you gain any insight as to who it was who had to give ultimate permission or authorisation for you to get through?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: The local checkpoint commander just walked away from us and came back at a later time, after some 10, 15 minutes, and then said we could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you arrived at Stupni Do, is it fair to say, sir, that the village was totally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Most definitely, it was pretty uninhabitable when we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based on what you had seen at Ahmici when you went there at the end of April, is it fair to say that in some sense, perhaps, Stupni Do was even worse than what you saw at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The destruction was complete in Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like the usher -- I apologise. I did not have a chance to copy these before. There are black and white Xerox copies that have been distributed so that everyone has them. Colour copies will be substituted, Your Honour. If you could just hand these to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By way of orientation, Major, you may have to look at the back of the photograph to get the number. They unfortunately have a tendency to stick together. If you can look first at Exhibit 2048,2, is that a photograph of at least part of the village after the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that essentially representative of what you saw throughout the entire village area?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The immediate thing which we noticed was the vast majority of roofs on the houses were non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that there were very few houses that had not been set on fire and totally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: That's right. The majority of them had no roofs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also encountered a number of bodies still in the area?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you relate to the Court any particular bodies that you saw which indicated to you that these were not deaths of combatants?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: There were three women in a vegetable pit in the cellar of a house. The bodies were still in there, the lid was open, and they had been killed what looked like inside where they were obviously hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you please look, with the usher's assistance, at Exhibit 2048,5? Tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. That's the area where we found the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're looking essentially down the length of something like a basement or cellar?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it may be difficult to tell with the ELMO, but can you point to approximately, because we're going to move in on this progressively closer, but with this larger view, can you point to the approximate area where the three women were found?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: In this area here [indicates] just by this green bucket in the corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you go to Exhibit Point 6, please? By that, I mean for the record Exhibit 2048,6. Again the ELMO makes it difficult. Now, can you see further the location of these three women?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, you can. You can see them just above the bucket here. And here is the lid which will be above the pit where they were hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you look at Exhibit 7.

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's a close-up of what we found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They were hiding in a basement and in a further enclosure under the floor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would you look finally at Exhibit 8. As you were in this cellar at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I am interrupting you for a moment to ask the Major whether he could tell us, in respect of this photograph and in respect of this exhibit, whether he knows how these three women were killed?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: We were told not to disturb any evidence, as war crimes investigators were going to arrive, but a cursory examination, certainly of these three, I felt that this woman here had had her throat cut and the other two had been stabbed and shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As you stood in that basement, sir, was there any indication, any evidence around these three women that they posed any military threat to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: No evidence which we could find at this particular site, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you attempted to leave Stupni Do later that day, is it correct, sir, that you were stopped again by an HVO checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. The same checkpoint that we had used to enter Stupni Do stopped us on our leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were they particularly hostile toward you leaving the area?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: They were very agitated and seemed to be more apprehensive rather than overtly aggressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did they take up firing positions against your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, they wanted to stop us leaving. And a young soldier had a rocket launcher on his shoulder, which to me indicated that -- and it was pointing in our direction, which indicated that he had taken up a firing position. And a number of them had cocked their weapons or made their weapons ready in front of us and were pointing them at us to try and enforce the point that we shouldn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Through your interpreter, were you able to determine that the soldiers were asking, wanting to know what had you been doing in the village, what had you seen, what were you doing up there?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes. That was the general line of the conversation to me through my interpreter, what were we doing here, what had we seen, what were we going to do. Generally along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By the fact of your being here, I guess we know you were ultimately able to leave the checkpoint; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. After some negotiation and being fairly forceful in our manner, we were allowed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In conclusion, then, Major Bower, was it your assessment and your experience throughout your six months in Central Bosnia that the HVO deliberately hindered and obstructed not only your efforts but the efforts of other humanitarian organisations to provide relief to Muslim civilians in Stari Vitez, in Kruscica and other locations?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again did this occur to you -- did this appear to you to be the acts of individual soldiers or was it not only your conclusion but the conclusion of the British Battalion that this was part of an organised, orchestrated campaign?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- it definitely seemed to be a policy which was applied and throughout the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you finally tell the Court, to your knowledge, sir, was there any military justification for denying or obstructing repeatedly your efforts to provide humanitarian aid to the Muslim civilians in these villages?

utterances.speaker: MARK WILLIAM BOWER
utterances.text: There was no reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, do you want to make a start now or would you prefer to leave it until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think tomorrow would be more than convenient, if that's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow. How long do you anticipate being with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think two hours, Your Honour, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what will be left for me, but I guess an hour, hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Major, we have to adjourn now. It's not possible for us to sit this afternoon because members of the Court are dealing with another case. So I must ask you to be back, please, tomorrow morning. I trust that we will conclude your evidence. If you'll be back at 9.30. Could you remember in this adjournment or in any others there may be, not to speak to anybody about your evidence, and that, of course, includes members of the Prosecution team. Thank you. We'll adjourn now until half past 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 12.53 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of November, 1999, at 9.30 a.m. 25
